intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to hold on to and shows where analysts slip. The section pages add a worked calculation, so do the arithmetic in pencil before you read the answer, then test yourself with the recall questions.

sections.title: Why cost-effectiveness?
sections.big_idea: Budgets are finite, so every rupee has an **opportunity cost**. Cost-effectiveness asks which option buys the most good per rupee.
in_plain_words: Every funder faces the same wall: there is never enough money to do everything worth doing. Cost-effectiveness is the discipline of choosing well under that limit. Its question is whether a programme does more good per rupee than the alternatives you could fund instead, which differs from asking whether it works. The true cost of programme A is the good programme B would have done.

Two programmes can both work and still differ tenfold in good per rupee, so cost-effective is a different thing from cheap. Users range from health ministries and India's HTA agency to funders, NGOs and global bodies. The tool informs and leaves out who is reached, rights and feasibility. In South Asia, low public spending and high out-of-pocket costs raise the stakes.

diagram.caption: the logic of the whole course in four steps

key_terms.meaning: Cost-effectiveness analysis: choosing the option with the most outcome per rupee.
The value of the best alternative you give up when you choose.
The alternative you measure against, such as current practice.
Total cost divided by total effect.
Health technology assessment, which appraises technologies for public financing.

worked_example.title: Same budget, two programmes
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: ₹10 lakh to spend. Programme A averts a case for ₹5,000 and programme B averts one for ₹500.
steps: The gap: 2,000 ÷ 200 = 10, so B averts ten times as many cases.
Both programmes work, so the comparison separates good from better.
Before accepting a tenfold gap, check that both ratios use the same perspective, outcome definition and time horizon.
worked_example.answer: Programme B averts 2,000 cases against 200, ten times as many for the same money.

mistakes: Equating cost-effective with cheap. The cheapest programme may deliver almost nothing.
Asking only whether a programme works, when the decision is which option does more good per rupee.
Leaving 'do nothing' and 'do the current thing better' off the option list.
Treating the ratio as the decision. Equity, rights, feasibility and politics also matter.

recall.q: What question does CEA answer?
recall.a: Which of these options does more good per rupee?

recall.q: Define opportunity cost.
recall.a: The value of the best alternative you give up when you choose one option.

recall.q: Why is delay a hidden cost?
recall.a: It shows as zero in the budget, yet it forgoes a year of outcomes.

recall.q: Why does the out-of-pocket row matter in South Asia?
recall.a: Where households pay directly, participant costs dominate, and a provider-perspective analysis omits most of the real cost.

sections.title: The family of methods
sections.big_idea: CEA, CUA and CBA share one ratio, **cost over outcome**. They differ in the unit of outcome, and each broader unit imports a value judgement.
in_plain_words: Economic evaluation has three main forms. CEA measures benefit in natural units such as cases averted and compares only programmes sharing that outcome. CUA uses DALYs or QALYs to compare across health conditions. CBA converts benefits to money, so it can compare a road with a clinic, at the price of pricing health and life. Cost-minimisation applies when two options give identical effects.

Choose the narrowest method that answers your question. Each step to a broader method adds a requirement: one clear natural unit, then disability weights and a threshold, then money values for non-market benefits. Never compare a CEA ratio with a CBA ratio, or ratios built on different perspectives, discount rates or horizons. **Report which method you used.**

diagram.note: natural units give CEA, DALYs or QALYs give CUA, money gives CBA

key_terms.meaning: Benefit in natural units; compares programmes with the same outcome.
A form of CEA using DALYs or QALYs, so health programmes compare on one scale.
Converts all benefits into money, giving a net benefit or benefit-cost ratio.
Picking the cheaper of two options with identical effects.
The outcome unit shifts, such as 'case detected' becoming 'case cured'.

worked_example.title: Pick the method
worked_example.setup: Use the table on slide 17 to choose a method for four comparisons.
steps: Three designs for raising immunisation coverage share a natural outcome, so use CEA.
A blindness programme against a diarrhoea programme crosses conditions, so use CUA with DALYs.
A rural road against a district hospital crosses sectors, so use CBA with money.
Two suppliers of an identical product have equal effects by assumption, so use cost-minimisation.
Then name what each method makes you supply: a unit, weights and a threshold, money values, or evidence of identical effects.
worked_example.answer: CEA, CUA, CBA and cost-minimisation, each the narrowest method that spans the options.

mistakes: Reaching for CBA when everyone shares one outcome. It adds contested monetisation and no extra comparison.
Comparing a CEA result for one programme with a CBA result for another.
Using cost-minimisation when effects are only 'roughly similar'. Nobody measured the difference.
Defining the outcome after collecting cost data, which invites defining it to suit the numbers.

recall.q: Which ratio do all four methods share?
recall.a: Cost over outcome. Only the denominator changes.

recall.q: Which method needs money values for non-market benefits?
recall.a: Cost-benefit analysis.

recall.q: What can CUA compare that CEA cannot?
recall.a: Programmes across different health conditions, because DALYs combine length and quality of life.

recall.q: Why is unit drift dangerous?
recall.a: Two programmes reported as 'cost per case' may count detection and cure, which a whole treatment cascade separates.

sections.title: Measuring costs
sections.big_idea: Real cost is a careful inventory priced at **opportunity cost**. Overheads, donated inputs and participants' time all belong in it.
in_plain_words: The figure on the grant agreement is rarely the real cost. The ingredients method lists every resource, quantifies it, prices it at its true value and sums it. Donated goods are priced at market value, volunteers at the wage they forgo and owned buildings at rental equivalent. Capital is annualised over its life. Every omission runs one way, so uncorrected estimates are optimistic.

Cost also depends on perspective. Provider, participant, health-system and societal views count different things, so say which you used. Participant costs such as lost wages, fares and childcare often exceed what the provider spends, and they explain why free services go unused. Fixed costs dominate in a pilot, so a pilot's ratio forecasts nothing about the scaled programme. **Separate fixed from variable.**

children.label: Indirect costs
items: Apportion them and state the basis

key_terms.meaning: List every resource, quantify it, price it at true value, then sum.
Shared support such as rent, accounts and IT; must be apportioned.
Does not change with scale, such as a training centre or vehicle.
Rises with each unit served, such as vaccines or stipends.
Whose costs are counted: provider, participant, health system or society.

worked_example.title: Build a total cost
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: other direct costs ₹8,00,000, out of ₹20,00,000 for all programmes sharing a ₹5,00,000 overhead pool. A vehicle cost ₹6,00,000, lasts 5 years and has ₹30,000 running costs. 1,000 participants lose ₹150 each.
steps: Vehicle per year: 6,00,000 ÷ 5 = 1,20,000.
Overhead share by direct cost: 8,00,000 ÷ 20,00,000 = 0.4.
Participant costs: 1,000 × 150 = 1,50,000.
worked_example.answer: ₹13,00,000. Overheads and participant costs, the two lines most often dropped, make up over a quarter of it.

mistakes: Charging a vehicle or building entirely to year one, which makes the pilot year look terrible and later years look artificially good.
Leaving overheads out because they sit in another budget line.
Reporting the pilot ratio as if it were the scaled programme's.
Counting provider costs only and calling the programme efficient when participants carry the burden.

recall.q: Give the four steps of the ingredients method.
recall.a: List every resource, quantify each, price each at its true value, and sum to a total.

recall.q: How are donated goods priced?
recall.a: At market price, never at zero.

recall.q: Why do pilots look expensive?
recall.a: Fixed costs are spread over few beneficiaries.

recall.q: Which perspective gives the fullest view, and what is its drawback?
recall.a: Societal, which counts all costs to anyone but is hardest to measure fully.

sections.title: Measuring effects
sections.big_idea: The effect is the **denominator**. Count outcomes the programme caused, against a counterfactual, and avoid outputs that are merely easy to count.
in_plain_words: Getting the denominator wrong does more damage than costing errors. Costing errors move a ratio by tens of per cent, while the wrong outcome can reverse a ranking. Natural units are intuitive, but weak ones such as people screened or taps installed are outputs. Climb the results chain from inputs to impact, and where you must cost an intermediate outcome, state the assumed link to the final one.

Attribution needs a counterfactual. Before-and-after change credits the programme with the trend, comparison with non-participants adds selection bias, quasi-experiments rest on assumptions and RCTs may not transfer. Monitoring data is available but has no counterfactual. A pooled estimate can average settings none of which is yours. **Carry the evidence's uncertainty into the ratio.**

diagram.caption: meaning rises and measurability falls as you climb

key_terms.meaning: What the programme delivers, such as nets distributed.
The change that follows, such as nets used nightly.
What would have happened without the programme.
Crediting the programme only with the change it caused.
A convenient stand-in for the outcome you care about.

worked_example.title: Check a cost per outcome
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a programme costs ₹6,00,000 and averts 300 cases. Run the four checks on slide 36.
steps: Cost per case averted: 6,00,000 ÷ 300 = 2,000.
Check the cost: which perspective, and were overheads and participant time included?
Check the effect: against what counterfactual were 300 cases averted?
Check the figure: is it an average or an incremental ratio?
Check the comparator: ₹2,000 against nothing is a different claim from ₹2,000 against current practice.
worked_example.answer: ₹2,000 per case averted, which stays incomplete until the comparator and counterfactual are stated.

mistakes: Costing outputs and calling them outcomes. An unused net averts nothing.
Dividing cost by the total change, which credits the programme with the trend.
Borrowing an RCT effect from elsewhere without adjusting for baseline burden, prices and delivery quality.
Reporting only the midpoint of a wide effect interval.

recall.q: What separates an output from an outcome?
recall.a: An output is what is delivered, such as nets distributed. An outcome is the change, such as nets used nightly.

recall.q: Why is the denominator more dangerous than the numerator?
recall.a: Costing errors move a ratio by tens of per cent, but the wrong outcome can move it by an order of magnitude and reverse a ranking.

recall.q: What counterfactual does a before-and-after comparison have?
recall.a: None. It assumes nothing else changed and credits the programme with the trend.

recall.q: Why is monitoring data unsuitable for effects?
recall.a: It records what happened to participants, which differs from what the programme caused.

sections.title: The cost-effectiveness ratio
sections.big_idea: Compare options with the **ICER**: extra cost over extra effect. An average ratio quietly flatters an upgrade.
in_plain_words: The CER is total cost over total effect, the average cost of one unit of outcome. It compares a programme with doing nothing, which is almost never the real alternative. The ICER divides the extra cost of switching from B to A by the extra effect gained, so it measures the upgrade. It inherits the uncertainty of both differences and becomes meaningless when the effect difference is near zero.

Start by eliminating dominated options: costs more and does less means drop it, and costs less and does more means adopt it. Compute ICERs for the hard middle, more cost and more effect, and judge them against a stated threshold. With several options, compute ICERs sequentially along the frontier. GDP-based thresholds are conventions and not findings, so **show results at other thresholds**.

left.title: Average CER
items: Cost of the whole programme per unit
Right for: whether to run it at all

right.title: ICER
items: Cost of the upgrade per extra unit

key_terms.meaning: Total cost divided by total effect; the average cost of one outcome.
Extra cost of switching from B to A divided by the extra effect gained.
An option that costs less and does more dominates; one costing more and doing less is dominated.
The most you will pay for one unit of outcome; a value judgement.
Surviving options by cost, each compared with the next cheapest.

worked_example.title: Average versus incremental
worked_example.setup: Illustrative, from slide 43: option B costs ₹5,00,000 for 200 cases and option A costs ₹8,00,000 for 260 cases.
steps: Extra effect of A: 260 − 200 = 60.
ICER: 3,00,000 ÷ 60 = 5,000 per extra case.
Compare with A's average: 5,000 ÷ 3,077 = 1.625, so the ICER is about 62% higher.
worked_example.answer: The upgrade costs ₹5,000 per extra case, about 62% above A's ₹3,077 average. The decision turns on the ₹5,000.

mistakes: Reporting the average CER when the decision is about an upgrade.
Comparing against 'nothing' when current practice is the real alternative.
Computing an ICER from a rounding-error difference in effect.
Leaving dominated options in, which produces ratios against an option nobody should choose.

recall.q: What does the ICER measure?
recall.a: The extra cost per extra unit of effect when switching from one option to another.

recall.q: What is a dominated option?
recall.a: One that costs more and does less. Drop it from the comparison.

recall.q: Why is the average CER no guide to scale-up?
recall.a: It says nothing about what reaching the next group would cost.

recall.q: With more than two options, how are ICERs computed?
recall.a: Sequentially along the efficiency frontier, each against the next cheapest surviving option.

sections.title: Cost-utility and DALYs
sections.big_idea: A DALY combines **dying early and living unwell** in one unit, so very different health programmes can be compared by cost per DALY averted.
in_plain_words: CEA cannot compare blindness prevention with child mortality, because the units differ. CUA solves that with a common currency of health, combining length and quality of life. A QALY counts health gained and a DALY counts health lost, so they are mirror images and must not be mixed in one calculation. A DALY is years of life lost plus years lived with disability.

Both halves embed value choices. YLL uses a reference life expectancy, so a childhood death counts more than one in old age. YLD uses disability weights from 0 to 1, drawn from surveys and contested by disability-rights scholars. Cost per DALY averted multiplies four uncertain estimates, so read it as an order of magnitude. **Never present a cost per DALY as a neutral fact.**

diagram.note: a DALY is a loss, so lower is better and programmes avert DALYs

key_terms.meaning: Disability-adjusted life year: one year of healthy life lost.
Quality-adjusted life year: one year of healthy life gained.
Reference life expectancy minus age at death.
Years with the condition times the disability weight.
A value from 0 (full health) to 1 (death) for a health state.

worked_example.title: From cases to cost per DALY
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: case A is a death at 30 with a reference life expectancy of 70. Case B is 5 years with a condition weighted 0.2. A programme costing ₹82,000 averts both.
steps: YLL for case A: 70 − 30 = 40.
YLD for case B: 5 × 0.2 = 1.
DALYs averted: 40 + 1 = 41.
Cost per DALY averted: 82,000 ÷ 41 = 2,000.
Report the life table and the weight used, since both are contestable.
worked_example.answer: 41 DALYs averted at ₹2,000 each, shown with the reference life expectancy and the weight.

mistakes: Mixing QALYs and DALYs in one calculation, or reading a QALY threshold as a DALY one.
Quoting a precise cost per DALY with no date, source or setting.
Treating a GDP-multiple threshold as an empirical finding.
Presenting disability weights as neutral measurements.

recall.q: What are the two halves of a DALY?
recall.a: Years of life lost to early death (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD).

recall.q: For QALYs and DALYs, is higher better?
recall.a: Higher is better for QALYs, which count health gained. Lower is better for DALYs, which count health lost.

recall.q: Why does a childhood death count for more than one in old age?
recall.a: YLL is anchored to a reference life expectancy, a deliberate value choice.

recall.q: What did the Global Burden of Disease study drop, and what followed?
recall.a: Age-weighting and discounting of years. The change moved disease rankings substantially.

sections.title: Time and discounting
sections.big_idea: A rupee today beats a rupee later. **Discount costs and benefits at a stated rate**, show other rates, and match the horizon to when effects occur.
in_plain_words: Discounting puts flows from different years on one footing. It reflects time preference, the return money could earn and uncertainty about the future. It is separate from inflation: work in real terms first, then discount, or you double-count. Present value is the future value divided by one plus the rate, raised to the number of years. Apply the same rate and convention to costs and benefits.

The rate has teeth. At 8% a benefit thirty years out is worth under a tenth of its face value, while at 3% it keeps over 40%, so prevention, education and climate work fare badly under high rates. Health is contested because it cannot be invested at a return. Report a base case at 3%, results at 0% and a higher rate, and the horizon, which the grant usually sets. **A hidden rate is a red flag.**

parts.hint: cost or benefit in year t

diagram.note: use a real rate, and apply the same one to costs and benefits

key_terms.meaning: The yearly rate that converts future value into present value.
What a future cost or benefit is worth today.
People generally prefer benefits now to benefits later.
Figures with price changes removed, discounted separately from inflation.
How many years of costs and benefits you include.

worked_example.title: Read the cost of a high rate
worked_example.setup: Use the table on slide 61 for ₹1,000 received in the future. The figures are the deck's.
steps: In year 10 it is worth about ₹744 at 3% and ₹463 at 8%.
The rate alone changes the value by 744 − 463 = 281.
In year 30 it is worth about ₹412 at 3% and ₹99 at 8%.
At 8%: 99 ÷ 1,000 = 0.099, under a tenth of face value.
At 3%: 412 ÷ 1,000 = 0.412, over 40% of face value.
worked_example.answer: The same benefit keeps 0.412 of its value at 3% and 0.099 at 8%, so a rate can flip a prevention decision.

mistakes: Applying a discount rate to nominal figures and then adjusting for inflation as well.
Discounting benefits but not costs, or using different rates for each.
Letting a three-year grant window set the horizon for a programme that pays off in adulthood.
Burying the rate. Report it with the horizon and show alternatives.

recall.q: What does present value tell you?
recall.a: What a future cost or benefit is worth today, after discounting.

recall.q: Why is discounting health more contested than discounting money?
recall.a: Health cannot be invested at a return, so the strongest argument for the rate does not carry across.

recall.q: Which rates does the deck suggest reporting?
recall.a: A base case at 3%, plus results at 0% and at a higher rate.

recall.q: What does a three-year horizon favour?
recall.a: Treatment and immediate delivery. It penalises prevention, education and infrastructure.

sections.title: Comparing interventions
sections.big_idea: A league table is only as honest as its **weakest entry**. Harmonise entries, show uncertainty, state context and pair the ranking with equity.
in_plain_words: Comparison is the payoff: laying interventions side by side to see where each rupee does most. It is valid only when entries share method, perspective, discount rate and horizon, outcome definitions and context. Harmonising entries is most of the work, and it is the part skipped when ratios are lifted from papers. If you cannot harmonise, present separate case studies and skip the ranked column.

Rankings hide uncertainty, and anything unmeasured counts as zero. The deworming debate shows the risk: a cheap, safe intervention topped league tables on a long-run effect estimate that later became disputed. A cheap numerator cannot rescue an uncertain denominator. Ratios also fail to transfer across settings, and marginal cost rises as you scale. **Fund the best buy up to a point, then move down the table.**

key_terms.meaning: A list of interventions ranked by cost-effectiveness ratio.
Whether a ratio from one setting holds in another.
Reaching each extra person tends to cost more.
How much money an efficient programme can actually use.
The cost of reaching the next person or group.

worked_example.title: Test a reallocation
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: programme A averts an outcome for ₹400 and programme E for ₹7,500. Someone proposes moving ₹7,50,000 from E to A.
steps: E today: 7,50,000 ÷ 7,500 = 100 outcomes.
A at the same ratio: 7,50,000 ÷ 400 = 1,875 outcomes.
The gap on paper: 7,500 ÷ 400 = 18.75 times as much per rupee.
Treat 1,875 as a ceiling, because marginal cost rises as easy cases are used up.
Ask the four questions on slide 70: same people, absorptive capacity, ratio at scale, what is lost when E closes.
worked_example.answer: On paper 1,875 outcomes against 100. The real gain is smaller and depends on the four questions.

mistakes: Lifting ratios from different papers into one ranked column.
Reading rank as precision when confidence intervals overlap heavily.
Borrowing a Kenyan or Bihar ratio for Odisha without recosting and re-estimating burden.
Pouring everything into the top entry. Returns diminish.

recall.q: Name three things every league table entry must share.
recall.a: Any three of: method, perspective, discount rate and horizon, outcome definition, context.

recall.q: Why can the order in a league table be noise?
recall.a: Where confidence intervals overlap heavily, the difference between places may be noise.

recall.q: What is the largest driver of transferability problems?
recall.a: Baseline disease burden.

recall.q: What does the deworming story say about CEA itself?
recall.a: Nothing against it. It says never read a league-table rank without its uncertainty.

recall.q: What happens to marginal cost as coverage grows?
recall.a: It rises as the easiest cases are used up, often to several times the average for the last 20%.

sections.title: Uncertainty and sensitivity
sections.big_idea: Every ratio is an estimate. **Show the range**, find which input swings the answer, and report the probability of good value.
in_plain_words: A ratio built from uncertain costs, effects and assumptions looks precise but is not. One-way sensitivity analysis varies a single input across a real range, from a confidence interval or observed site variation, and shows which assumptions the answer hinges on. A tornado diagram sorts the swings, and effect size usually tops it. If no bar crosses the threshold line, the conclusion holds up, which is a finding.

Probabilistic analysis varies all inputs together from distributions, simulating thousands of runs. Plot results on the cost-effectiveness plane with extra effect across and extra cost up. Upper right needs a threshold, lower right is dominant and upper left is dominated. Report the share of simulations below the threshold, or an acceptability curve. **The width of the range is often the most decision-relevant fact.**

diagram.caption: from one input to the whole picture

key_terms.meaning: Asking how far a result could move when inputs change.
Varying one input at a time across a plausible range.
Bars sorted widest to narrowest by swing in the result.
Probabilistic sensitivity analysis: all inputs vary together from distributions.
Extra effect against extra cost relative to the comparator.
The probability of good value across a range of thresholds.

worked_example.title: Compare two ranges
worked_example.setup: From slide 83: interventions X and Y both have a point estimate of ₹5,000. X ranges from ₹4,500 to ₹5,500 and Y from ₹900 to ₹40,000. The threshold is ₹10,000.
steps: Width of X's range: 5,500 − 4,500 = 1,000.
Width of Y's range: 40,000 − 900 = 39,100.
Y's range is wider by 39,100 ÷ 1,000 = 39.1 times.
X's whole range sits below ₹10,000, so X is near certain good value.
Y's range straddles ₹10,000, so it is roughly a coin toss.
worked_example.answer: Same headline ratio, different decisions. Report the range and the probability, and consider buying better evidence on Y.

mistakes: Using a tidy ±20% instead of a range from the confidence interval or observed variation.
Running sensitivity analysis as a box-ticking ritual after the answer is chosen.
Treating a narrow tornado as no result. A stable conclusion is a finding.
Quoting a single ICER from a simulation cloud that spans quadrants.

recall.q: What does the widest tornado bar show?
recall.a: The input that drives the answer most.

recall.q: What does a bar crossing the threshold line mean?
recall.a: That input alone can flip the decision.

recall.q: How does PSA differ from one-way analysis?
recall.a: PSA varies all inputs together from distributions and gives a distribution of results. One-way analysis varies one input at a time.

recall.q: What does an acceptability curve show?
recall.a: The probability of good value across thresholds, so you need not commit to one.

sections.title: Limits and equity
sections.big_idea: Cost-effectiveness settles **one question well**: outcomes per rupee. Distribution, rights, dignity and the unmeasured need other tools.
in_plain_words: The ratio is a total divided by a total, and totals cannot express distribution. Rights, dignity in process and political feasibility lie outside it. Cost per outcome and need run in opposite directions: reaching a remote Adivasi hamlet or a person with disability costs more per outcome, so unweighted analysis points away from the worst-off. Reporting outcomes by group beside the ratio is the cheapest equity correction.

Equity weighting counts an outcome for a worse-off person as worth more, which makes the value judgement visible and arguable, though the weights are a political and ethical choice. Disability weights, discount rates, thresholds, the choice of outcome and the perspective all encode values. Anything unmeasured is treated as worth zero, so **list what you could not quantify** next to the ratio.

right.title: What stays open
items: Dignity in how people are treated

key_terms.meaning: Counting an outcome for a worse-off person as worth more.
Reports outcomes by group instead of in one total.
Something the ratio cannot express, such as distribution or process.
People costing more per outcome to serve, so easily deprioritised.
Dignity, voice or cohesion, treated by the ratio as worth zero.

worked_example.title: Can the ratio weigh it?
worked_example.setup: Sort five values with the table on slide 85.
steps: Outcomes per rupee: yes, this is what CEA measures.
Fairness in who receives: only if you add equity weights.
Rights and legal obligation: no, obligations do not depend on ratios.
Dignity in how people are treated: no, process is invisible to the ratio.
Political feasibility: no. Present these beside the ratio.
worked_example.answer: Only efficiency, and fairness with equity weights. Everything else needs deliberation beside the ratio.

mistakes: Reading the ratio's silence as the other values having no weight.
Presenting a ranking without the distribution alongside it.
Treating the equity weight as a technical fact when it is a political and ethical choice.
Leaving out dignity, voice and cohesion, which the arithmetic values at zero.

recall.q: Why does unweighted CEA point away from the worst-off?
recall.a: Cost per outcome and need run in opposite directions, so the cheapest outcomes are in accessible places.

recall.q: What does equity weighting make you state?
recall.a: Who counts as worse-off, how much extra weight, whose judgement sets it, and whether the ranking survives other weights.

recall.q: What is the cheapest equity correction?
recall.a: Reporting outcomes by group alongside the aggregate ratio.

recall.q: How does the arithmetic treat an omitted benefit?
recall.a: Exactly as if it had been measured and found to be nothing.

sections.title: Practice and tools
sections.big_idea: Pin down **cost, effect, comparator and assumptions** before you compute. Most disputes about a result are disputes about those choices.
in_plain_words: A cost-effectiveness study needs a full ingredients inventory, a credible causal effect estimate, a comparator and openly stated assumptions on discount rate, horizon and perspective. Write them as a table at the front of any analysis. Most arguments trace back to these five choices and seldom to the arithmetic.

Start in a spreadsheet. Keep one assumption per labelled cell, no constants hidden in formulas, separate sheets for costs, effects and results, and a sensitivity tab built before the results are known. When you read someone else's work, watch for a single ratio with no range, an average where an ICER was needed, no stated perspective, one study treated as settled, and a ranking that ignores who is missed. **Ask for the model and read it before the summary.**

key_terms.meaning: What you measure against, such as current practice or nothing.
A reporting statement and checklist for what an analysis must disclose.
A spreadsheet with each assumption in one labelled cell.
A pattern that calls for a question and proves nothing alone.
A shared standard for credible economic evaluation.

worked_example.title: Read a summary with the red flags
worked_example.setup: An invented summary says: 'Programme Z costs ₹2,000 per case averted and beats all others.' Check it against slide 96.
steps: A single ratio with no range: ask for the uncertainty.
An average where an ICER was needed: ask what it was compared with.
No stated perspective: assume participant costs were excluded until shown otherwise.
One study treated as settled: ask whether the effect has replicated.
A ranking with no distributional data: ask who is not reached.
worked_example.answer: None of this proves an error. Ask for the model, because the missing information is what would let you disagree.

mistakes: Hard-coding constants inside formulas, where they become the commonest source of error.
Adding sensitivity analysis after the results, which invites ranges that keep the answer where it was.
Treating red flags as accusations. Any one of them can be innocent.
Reporting the headline ratio without the five stated choices behind it.

recall.q: What does a cost-effectiveness study need?
recall.a: A full cost inventory, a causal effect estimate, a comparator, and stated assumptions on discount rate, horizon and perspective.

recall.q: Why build the sensitivity tab first?
recall.a: Retrofitting one means rebuilding the model, and building it afterwards invites choosing ranges that keep the answer in place.

recall.q: Name two red flags when reading a CEA.
recall.a: A single ratio with no range; an average where an ICER was needed; no stated perspective; one study treated as settled; a ranking that ignores who is missed.

recall.q: What is CHEERS good for?
recall.a: It is a reporting checklist you can run over an analysis you are reading or writing.

notes.2: The agenda has eleven topics, from why we compare to how to build the model. Note the order: costs, then effects, then the ratio, then DALYs and time, then comparison and uncertainty, with limits and equity near the end. Keep that order in mind as a map of the whole course.
notes.4: Read the two columns as the boundary of the method. It answers which option does more good per rupee. It leaves open whether the outcome is the right one to want and who should receive it. Those are value questions, so **name the outcome, cost every ingredient and state the comparator** first.
notes.5: Opportunity cost is the best alternative you give up. The last row of the table is the one that never appears in a budget: **delay is a choice with a cost**. If you cannot say what the alternative is, you have not yet stated the cost of your choice.
notes.6: Follow the four steps from a fixed budget to a decision. Step two is where analyses go wrong, because a list drawn up in advance only ranks what someone already thought of. Add **'do nothing' and 'do the current thing better'** to every option list.
notes.7: Work the arithmetic yourself. The table is right: ₹10 lakh at ₹5,000 a case buys 200 cases, and at ₹500 it buys 2,000. The text above says 20 where the table says 2,000, so trust the table. The tenfold gap is the point, though **a gap this size is often partly methodological**.
notes.8: Keep cost and outcome together. In the table the most expensive programme is the most cost-effective, **eight times better** than the cheapest. Total cost tells you what fits the budget and says nothing about value. Watch the opposite trap too: a low unit cost reached by serving only the easiest cases.
notes.9: Find yourself in the table. Health ministries, India's HTA agency, funders, NGOs and global bodies all ask the same question at different scales. At a panchayat or district the arithmetic is simpler and the discipline stays the same: **name the options, cost them fully, agree the outcome and say who each reaches**.
notes.10: The ratio is one input. Equity, rights, feasibility and politics sit beside it. Present the ratio alongside those considerations and avoid leading with it, since a number shown first anchors the discussion. Its strongest use is diagnostic: a programme that looks far worse than its peers often has **a design problem worth fixing**.
notes.11: The third row of the table is the distinctive one. Where households pay a large share of health costs directly, a provider-perspective analysis misses most of the real cost. A programme that cuts out-of-pocket spending can look like **pure cost to a provider** and still be cost-effective for society.
notes.13: Three cousins, one ratio. Read the table left to right: as the denominator becomes more universal, comparison scope grows and so does the hazard. **Choose the narrowest method that answers your question**, because reaching for CBA when everyone shares one outcome adds contested monetisation and no extra comparison.
notes.14: CEA keeps the outcome in real units, which practitioners trust, but only programmes sharing that outcome can be compared. The quiet killer is **unit drift**: 'case detected' and 'case cured' sit a whole treatment cascade apart. Define the outcome in one sentence before you collect any cost data.
notes.15: CUA is CEA with a common health unit. Because a DALY captures both length and quality of life, you can ask whether a rupee does more against blindness, diarrhoea or heart disease. Remember it as **the bridge between diseases**. Section 6 covers it in detail.
notes.16: CBA puts everything in rupees, so a road, a school and a clinic share one common unit. The price is uncomfortable assumptions. The serious objection in the table is income: **willingness-to-pay makes poorer lives price lower**. Use CBA where only money can span sectors, and prefer CEA inside one sector.
notes.17: Use the lower table as a quick chooser: match the comparison you need to the method that spans it. The footnote matters. Cost-minimisation is valid only when effects are equal, and **'roughly similar' usually means nobody measured the difference**. Pick the method from the question and let your available data follow.
notes.18: This is the same chooser as a set of questions. The right-hand column of the table is what you must supply once you pick a method, and each entry is more contestable than a natural unit. The default is **the narrowest method that spans your options**.
notes.19: Remember the whole family as one line: cost divided by outcome. The numerator is always cost, and only the denominator changes. When two analyses disagree, ask first what each put on the bottom line.
notes.20: The method is a lens, so say which one you used. The table lists comparisons to refuse: CEA against CBA, provider against societal costs, different discount rates, and an average CER against an ICER. If you cannot harmonise entries, **present them separately** with a footnote about incomparability.
notes.22: The grant agreement is not the cost. The table lists what is routinely left out, and every omission runs the same way, so uncorrected estimates are **systematically optimistic**. Take special care comparing an NGO pilot with a government programme, since the pilot may run on donated inputs the state would have to buy.
notes.23: Use four steps: list, quantify, price, sum. 'True value' means opportunity cost, which differs from what appeared on an invoice. Annualise capital instead of charging it all to year one, or **the pilot year looks terrible and every later year looks artificially good**.
notes.24: Leaving out indirect costs is the commonest way to flatter a programme, and it is rarely deliberate because overheads sit in another budget line. Whatever basis you choose to apportion them, **state it**. Two organisations using different bases report different unit costs for identical work.
notes.25: Split costs into fixed and variable and the pilot puzzle resolves. Fixed costs dominate at pilot size and shrink per beneficiary at scale, while variable costs dominate later. **A pilot's ratio is not a forecast** of the scaled programme's. Show both numbers to any funder deciding on scale-up.
notes.26: Read the curve for its shape and treat the values as illustrative. Fixed costs spread over more people, so cost per beneficiary falls steeply, then flattens. When a pilot ratio looks poor, ask **where on this curve the programme sits** before judging it.
notes.27: Perspective decides what counts, so state it in the first line of the methods. Provider, participant, health system and societal views each omit something. A programme that shifts cost onto participants looks efficient from the provider side. **Two ratios from different perspectives cannot be compared.**
notes.28: For a daily-wage worker a 'free' camp costs a day's wage, bus fare and childcare. These participant costs are the main reason free services go unused, and ignoring them makes low uptake look like a behaviour problem. Designs that cut them, such as **doorstep delivery or evening timings**, often improve the ratio most.
notes.29: The chart is illustrative, but the lesson is concrete: overheads and participant time together are nearly a quarter of cost, and leaving them out makes the programme look about 23% cheaper than it is. Both are hard to see from inside the organisation, so **ask for them by name**.
notes.31: Cost is the numerator and effect is the denominator, and the denominator does more damage. Costing errors move a ratio by tens of per cent, while the wrong outcome can reverse a ranking. Ask what would have to be true for **this denominator to be what you actually care about**.
notes.32: Every weak unit in the right-hand column is an output, and outputs are cheaper and easier to count. That asymmetry pulls reporting towards them. Check the word 'sustained' in the water row: a tap that fails in eighteen months and a tap maintained for a decade are **the same output and different outcomes**.
notes.33: Measurability and meaning run in opposite directions, so programmes drift up the chain towards outputs without anyone being dishonest. If you must cost an intermediate outcome, **state the assumed link to the final one** and test it in sensitivity analysis.
notes.34: Walk down the chain from inputs to impact and ask which step your monitoring system reaches. Costing nets distributed is cheap, but an unused net averts nothing. Go one step beyond your data and model the conversion explicitly, since **that conversion rate is usually the largest uncertainty**.
notes.35: A cost-effectiveness ratio needs the effect the programme caused, so you need a counterfactual. Read the table as a ladder from weak to strong. Before-and-after comparison credits the programme with the trend. Monitoring data is the easiest source and the **least suitable** one.
notes.36: Divide total cost by total effect and you get cost per outcome: ₹6 lakh over 300 cases is ₹2,000. Then run the four checks in the table. If three are unanswerable from the document, **that tells you how much weight the figure can bear**. A ratio with no comparator is incomplete.
notes.37: An effect estimate is only as good as its evidence. The second table says when to use each source and what to adjust for. Look at the spread across studies as well as the central estimate, and **carry the uncertainty into the ratio** so a wide interval does not shrink to a midpoint.
notes.38: Check the denominator first when you compare published ratios. The same programme can report four ratios orders of magnitude apart, all arithmetically correct, depending on whether it divides by leaflets, people trained, practice changed or health improved. Ask whether yours is **a real outcome or a convenient proxy**.
notes.40: The CER is average cost per unit of outcome, and lower is better only inside a valid comparison. Read the right-hand column as what the ratio assumes. The fourth row is why the CER cannot guide scale-up: **average cost says nothing about the next group**.
notes.41: Compare the two columns. The average CER sets a programme against doing nothing, which is almost never the real alternative. The honest comparator is current practice. **Naming the comparator is half the analysis**, since the same intervention gives different ratios against different comparators.
notes.42: The ICER is extra cost divided by extra effect between two options, so it measures the upgrade. Because it is a ratio of two differences it inherits both uncertainties, and a near-zero effect difference makes it meaningless. **Report the incremental cost and effect separately** beside the ratio.
notes.43: Work the table. Option A averages ₹3,077 per case, yet its incremental ratio against B is ₹5,000, which is 62% higher. The decision is about the upgrade, so **₹5,000 is the number that matters**. Strong baselines make every improvement costly at the margin, and averages conceal it.
notes.44: Compute the ICER in one line: ₹3,00,000 extra cost divided by 60 extra cases is ₹5,000 each. Then ask the funder's four questions. The second changes answers most often: **detection without treatment averts nothing**, and an upgrade that detects more without linking to treatment has bought a statistic.
notes.45: An ICER means something only against a threshold. The table lists four ways to set one, each with a problem. The last is correct in principle: the health displaced elsewhere. If you use a GDP multiple, **say it is a convention and not a finding**, and show other thresholds.
notes.46: Sort options by cost and effect before computing anything. Lower cost and higher effect means adopt. Higher cost and lower effect means drop. Only the upper-right and lower-left rows need an ICER. **Eliminate dominated options first**, so ratios are not computed against an option nobody should choose.
notes.47: Match the question to the number. Whether to run a programme at all takes the average against the status quo. Whether to upgrade takes the ICER. With several options, compute ICERs **along the frontier**, each against the next cheapest survivor. Reporting an average for an upgrade is the costliest slip.
notes.49: CEA cannot compare blindness with child deaths because the units differ. Use the table to see which comparison needs which method. The third row is what the DALY was built for: a measure combining **length and quality of life**. Combining them requires disability weights, and those are contested.
notes.50: QALYs count health gained and DALYs count health lost, so they are near mirror images. Do not mix them in one calculation. Check which your source used before quoting a threshold, because **a QALY figure cannot be read across as DALYs**. The weights come from different populations.
notes.51: A DALY is a year of healthy life lost: years of life lost plus years lived with disability. Because it is a loss, programmes **avert** DALYs. A programme averting 500 DALYs prevented 500 years of healthy life from being lost, and added none to anyone.
notes.52: Take the two halves apart. YLL is a death at 30 against a life expectancy of 70, which loses 40 years. YLD weights years in ill health by severity. YLL embeds a value choice: **a childhood death counts far more than one in old age**.
notes.53: Each condition has a weight from 0 to 1. The weights come from surveys and are standardised and contested. The table gives four objections. You can use DALYs and hold the critique, but **do not present a cost-per-DALY figure as neutral fact**, because the weights are values.
notes.54: Cost per DALY averted works across completely different diseases. It multiplies four estimates: cost, cases averted, DALYs per case, and a horizon and rate. Uncertainties compound, so read a published figure as **an order of magnitude**. Two- or three-fold differences between studies are common.
notes.55: The bars show ordering only, so avoid quoting figures from them. Childhood vaccination, bed nets and vitamin A are commonly cited cheap buys, each with a caveat. **Every entry is conditional on its setting**: bed nets are an excellent buy where malaria is endemic and a poor one where it is not.
notes.56: A threshold of one to three times GDP per capita is a rule of thumb and has never been an empirical finding. WHO has moved away from it. It rises with national income and has no link to the health budget. Treat any threshold as **one input and never a verdict**.
notes.58: A rupee in hand today can be invested and is certain. Discounting puts flows from different years on one footing. Keep it separate from inflation: these are real rupees in both years. **Discounting nominal figures double-counts.** Get this distinction right before anything else in the section.
notes.59: Three reasons to discount: time preference, opportunity cost of capital and uncertainty. The table shows why discounting money is uncontroversial and health is not, since health cannot be invested at a return. Work in real terms first, then discount, and **never fold both into one rate**.
notes.60: Present value is future value divided by one plus the rate, raised to the number of years. Read the table for where slips occur: use a real rate, and apply the same rate and convention to **costs and benefits alike**. Different rates for each produce a ratio that means nothing.
notes.61: Read the table as well as the chart. At 8% a benefit thirty years out is worth about a tenth of its face value. At 3% it keeps over 40%. Prevention, education and climate work pay off late, so **a high rate penalises exactly them**.
notes.62: The rate is partly an ethical parameter: a high rate says a life saved in forty years counts for a fraction of one saved now. Follow the slide's advice. **Report the base case at 3%, show 0% and a higher rate**, and say plainly if the decision flips between them.
notes.63: Three positions on discounting health, each with a problem. The 'indefinite delay' paradox is the standard argument for discounting: if future health is not discounted, waiting a year costs nothing and so does waiting forever. There is no settled answer, so **say what you did and show the alternatives**.
notes.64: The horizon is how many years you count, and the grant usually sets it. A three-year window on a programme that pays off in adulthood measures the wrong period and reports failure. **Choose the horizon from the causal chain**, and model both if the funder's window is shorter.
notes.65: Treat the discount rate as the most powerful and least visible assumption. Report four things together: base-case rate, why that rate, results at other rates, and the horizon. An analysis with a long horizon and **no stated rate cannot be evaluated**, so ask for the model.
notes.67: This is the payoff of all the standardising. A valid comparison needs the same method, perspective, rate and horizon, outcome definition and context. Most of the work in a league table is **harmonising entries**. If you cannot, attach assumptions to each entry and skip the ranking.
notes.68: A league table ranks by cost-effectiveness ratio. Test one with the four questions in the table. The fourth is the most important and least asked: anything nobody measured, such as dignity or cohesion, is absent and so, in effect, **valued at zero**. Ranks also imply precision the estimates rarely have.
notes.69: Funders such as GiveWell rank charities by cost per comparable outcome. The chart is illustrative. The table shows that trust depends on uncertainty per entry. Imitate the practice of **publishing the model with its judgement calls visible**, since a bare list of positions is an argument and falls short of evidence.
notes.70: The slide gives a tempting comparison: ₹400 against ₹7,500 per outcome. Read the table before you move money. Efficiency gains can come from dropping the hardest to reach, the efficient programme may be unable to absorb the money, and its ratio may fail at scale. Cost-effectiveness tells you **where to look harder**.
notes.71: Use deworming as a cautionary tale. The pills are cheap and safe, yet the size of the long-run benefit became disputed after replication and review. The honest summary is that the effect size is contested. Both 'best buy' and 'debunked' overstate it, and the **failure was in the effect estimate**.
notes.72: Keep four lessons: a ranking is only as solid as its effect estimate, one influential study can move millions, a cheap numerator cannot rescue an uncertain denominator, and precise ratios hide wide ranges. The slide says nothing against CEA itself: **never read a rank without its uncertainty**.
notes.73: A ratio from Kenya or Bihar will not automatically hold in Odisha or Sindh. Baseline burden is the largest driver and the most forgotten. Before borrowing, **recost the numerator with local prices and re-estimate the denominator with local burden**. Trial-quality delivery rarely survives scale-up either.
notes.74: The best buy changes as you scale. The table shows the first 50% of coverage costing little, the next 30% more, and the last 20% often several times the average. Decisions about scale-up need the **marginal ratio**. This is also where efficiency and equity collide, since the last 20% are the poorest.
notes.75: Five habits: same method, units, perspective and rate for every entry; uncertainty per entry; context for each estimate; equity beside the ranking; and a list of what could not be quantified. None needs new data. If a table cannot satisfy the first, **present separate case studies** instead of a ranking.
notes.77: Every ratio is an estimate, so demand the range. The table shows the usual biggest drivers: effect size, then discount rate over long horizons, then coverage. The input that swings the answer most is **where better evidence is worth buying**. A point estimate with no uncertainty is a claim and falls short of a result.
notes.78: One-way analysis varies one input at a time across a real range. If halving the effect doubles the cost per outcome and flips your decision, you have found the input to study. Draw ranges from **confidence intervals or observed site variation**, never a tidy ±20%, and act on what the right-hand column says.
notes.79: Read a tornado by its widest bar at the top and by whether a bar crosses the threshold line, since that input alone can flip the decision. Values are illustrative. If all bars are narrow, the conclusion holds up, and **a stable result is a finding** worth reporting.
notes.80: One-way analysis finds the drivers. PSA gives each input a distribution and simulates thousands of runs, which answers the question decision-makers actually ask: how likely is this option to be the best buy? Run both, because one-way analysis **understates total uncertainty**.
notes.81: Plot extra effect across and extra cost up, with the comparator at the origin. Lower right is dominant, upper left is dominated, and the other two depend on the threshold. Most real comparisons land upper right, so the threshold line is a value judgement. If a PSA cloud spans quadrants, report **the share below the threshold**.
notes.82: Each dot is one simulation, and the threshold line runs from the origin. Read the cloud: a tight cluster below the line is confident good value, and a wide cloud straddling it is uncertain. The useful output is a probability a committee can act on, and an **acceptability curve** shows it across thresholds.
notes.83: Compare X and Y: same point estimate, entirely different decisions. X is near certain below a ₹10,000 threshold and Y is roughly a coin toss. The point estimate is the least informative number quoted. When the range is wide, **buy better evidence** before you decide.
notes.85: Efficiency is one value among several. Use the table to see what CEA can and cannot weigh: it handles outcomes per rupee, fairness only with equity weights, and nothing on rights, dignity or feasibility. **When the ratio is silent on a value, that value still counts.**
notes.86: The ratio is a total divided by a total, and totals cannot express distribution. Each blind spot in the table is structural. The cheapest fix covers the first and fourth: **report outcomes by group alongside the aggregate ratio**. It costs almost nothing.
notes.87: Cost per outcome and need run in opposite directions, so unweighted cost-effectiveness points away from the worst-off. Remote Adivasi hamlets and people with disabilities cost most to reach. Never present the ranking without the distribution beside it. Efficiency still deserves measuring, and **this is the field's central ethical tension**.
notes.88: Equity weighting counts an outcome for a worse-off person as worth more. Its advantage is that the value judgement becomes visible and arguable. The table lists what you must state: who is worse-off, how much extra weight, whose judgement sets it, and whether the ranking survives other weights. **Choosing weights is a political act.**
notes.89: Every technical choice encodes a value: disability weights, discount rate, threshold, outcome and perspective. None can be derived from data. Publish the assumptions prominently and show how the conclusion moves when a reader substitutes their own. **Read the choices as well as the digits.**
notes.90: What gets measured gets funded. Dignity, women's voice, cohesion, resilience and institutional capacity are treated as worth zero when nobody quantifies them. An omitted benefit counts in the arithmetic as if measured and found to be nothing, so **list what you could not quantify** next to the ratio.
notes.91: Use CEA as a discipline of attention. The table shows the habits it forces: name the outcome, cost every ingredient, name the comparator, state assumptions. Most of the value arrives before the division. Present the result beside equity, rights and feasibility, and **let deliberation make the final call**.
notes.93: Pin down your inputs before you compute. The list gives four items and the table gives five rows, because assumptions split into rate and horizon plus perspective. Most disputes trace back to one of these. Write them as a table at the front of any analysis you produce.
notes.94: Start in a spreadsheet and favour clarity over sophistication. Keep each assumption in one labelled cell, hard-code nothing in formulas, and split costs, effects and results onto separate sheets. **Build the sensitivity tab first**, before the results are known, so you cannot pick ranges that keep the answer where it was.
notes.95: Five habits make an analysis trustworthy: state perspective, comparator, horizon and rate; use the ingredients method; report ICERs beside averages; show sensitivity analysis; present equity beside efficiency. None needs new data. Run the **CHEERS statement** over your draft before circulation to catch what a reviewer would raise.
notes.96: Read the red flags as questions and take none as an accusation. Any one can be innocent, but each leaves out exactly the information that would let you disagree. Make it a habit to **ask for the model before you trust the summary**. An analyst who shares the spreadsheet is making a different claim.
notes.97: Use the second table to choose a source. Drummond is the standard textbook, WHO-CHOICE and DCP3 give comparable estimates, and GiveWell shows assumptions exposed. CHEERS is the most immediately useful, because you can run the checklist over an analysis you are reading as easily as one you are writing.
notes.98: Cost-effectiveness is strongest when fed by good measurement, sound evaluation and honest data. The slide pairs it with ImpactMojo's Data Literacy, Impact Evaluation and Theory of Change courses. Pick the one that fills the weakest input to your own analysis.
notes.99: Five takeaways, each tied to the mistake it prevents. Several are about how a result is reported, and that is where most of the damage is done. If you keep one habit, keep **the comparator**: asking 'compared with what?' of any ratio will expose more weak analysis than any other question.
